turns.prompt_text: I'm using karabiner elements on my macbook air, I would like to use the right command key as an undo button and the right option key as a paste button when tapped, they can do their original function if they are held down instead of tapped
turns.response_html:
To achieve this in Karabiner-Elements, you'll need to use Complex Modifications. Since Karabiner's internal logic distinguishes between a "hold" and a "tap" (using to_if_alone and to_if_held_down), we can map these keys to trigger Command + Z (Undo) and Command + V (Paste) specifically when they are tapped.

The Logic Breakdown

For both keys, we are defining two behaviors:

  1. to_if_alone: Triggers when you press and release the key quickly (the "Tap").
  2. to_if_held_down: Triggers the original modifier function if you hold it or use it in combination with another key.

The JSON Configuration

You will need to add the following code to your karabiner.json file (typically found at ~/.config/karabiner/karabiner.json) under the rules section of your profile:

{
  "description": "Right Command = Undo on tap, Right Option = Paste on tap",
  "manipulators": [
    {
      "type": "basic",
      "from": {
        "key_code": "right_command",
        "modifiers": { "optional": ["any"] }
      },
      "to_if_alone": [
        {
          "key_code": "z",
          "modifiers": ["left_command"]
        }
      ],
      "to_if_held_down": [
        { "key_code": "right_command" }
      ]
    },
    {
      "type": "basic",
      "from": {
        "key_code": "right_option",
        "modifiers": { "optional": ["any"] }
      },
      "to_if_alone": [
        {
          "key_code": "v",
          "modifiers": ["left_command"]
        }
      ],
      "to_if_held_down": [
        { "key_code": "right_option" }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

How to Install This

  1. Open Karabiner-Elements Settings.
  2. Go to the Complex Modifications tab.
  3. Instead of manually editing the JSON (which can be risky if you miss a comma), you can use the "Add rule" button.
  4. If you prefer a GUI approach, you can visit the Karabiner Complex Modifications website, but since this is a specific custom request, manual entry into your karabiner.json is usually the most direct path.

A Quick Tip for Your Workflow

Since you're working on a MacBook Air, you might find that the "held down" timing feels a bit slow or too fast. You can fine-tune this in the Parameters tab of Karabiner-Elements by adjusting the to_if_alone_timeout_milliseconds. The default is usually 1000ms, but many people prefer around 500ms for a snappier feel.

Would you like me to help you format a full karabiner.json file if you're having trouble figuring out exactly where to paste that block?

turns.prompt_text: I'd like to keep this modular
turns.response_html:
To keep your configuration modular and avoid cluttering your main karabiner.json with a massive block of text, you can create a standalone JSON file. This allows you to "import" the rule through the Karabiner-Elements GUI whenever you need it.

Step 1: Create the Modular File

Create a new file in the Karabiner configuration directory. Open your terminal and run:

touch ~/.config/karabiner/assets/complex_modifications/tap_mods.json

Step 2: Paste the Configuration

Paste the following code into that tap_mods.json file. This structure includes the necessary title and rules wrappers that Karabiner looks for when importing.

{
  "title": "My Custom Tap Modifiers",
  "rules": [
    {
      "description": "Right Command as Undo, Right Option as Paste (Tap vs Hold)",
      "manipulators": [
        {
          "type": "basic",
          "from": {
            "key_code": "right_command",
            "modifiers": { "optional": ["any"] }
          },
          "to_if_alone": [
            {
              "key_code": "z",
              "modifiers": ["left_command"]
            }
          ],
          "to_if_held_down": [
            { "key_code": "right_command" }
          ]
        },
        {
          "type": "basic",
          "from": {
            "key_code": "right_option",
            "modifiers": { "optional": ["any"] }
          },
          "to_if_alone": [
            {
              "key_code": "v",
              "modifiers": ["left_command"]
            }
          ],
          "to_if_held_down": [
            { "key_code": "right_option" }
          ]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Step 3: Enable the Rule via GUI

By placing the file in the assets/complex_modifications folder, it will now appear as an option in the app:

  1. Open Karabiner-Elements Settings.
  2. Navigate to Complex Modifications.
  3. Click Add rule.
  4. You will see "My Custom Tap Modifiers" (the title we gave the file) in the list.
  5. Click Enable next to the rule.

Why this is better for your setup:

  • Portability: You can easily move this single file to another Mac without digging through your entire system config.
  • Organization: If you decide you don't like the "tap to paste" behavior later, you can disable it in the GUI without deleting any code.
  • Debugging: If you have a syntax error (like a missing comma), it will only break this modular file, not your entire Karabiner configuration.

Since you're using a MacBook Air and likely rely on the internal keyboard often, would you like me to show you how to limit these rules so they only apply to your laptop keyboard and not an external one?

For the "Paste without formatting" exception, we add a specific manipulator that looks for the shift modifier alongside your left_command.

turns.prompt_text: In fish terminal, let's have every command auto control-l for clear screen
turns.response_html:
In the Fish shell, you can achieve this by using the fish_preexec event. This event triggers a function right after you hit Enter but before the command actually executes.

By adding a clear command to this event, you will get that fresh-screen feel every time you run a command.

The Fish Configuration

Add the following function to your config.fish file (usually located at ~/.config/fish/config.fish):

function clear_before_command --on-event fish_preexec
    # This simulates the Ctrl+L (clear) behavior
    clear
end

How to apply it:

  1. Open your config file: nano ~/.config/fish/config.fish
  2. Paste the function at the bottom.
  3. Save and exit.
  4. Restart your terminal or run source ~/.config/fish/config.fish.

A "Software Engineer" Refinement

Since you are a software engineer, you might find that clearing the screen every single time makes it difficult to reference the output of the previous command (like copying an error message into a file or checking a git hash).

If you want a "clean" look without losing your history entirely, you could use a divider instead of a full clear. This visually separates commands while keeping your logs accessible:

function divide_commands --on-event fish_preexec
    echo (set_color yellow)"------------------------------------------------"(set_color normal)
end

Potential Conflicts

Since we just set up Karabiner-Elements to handle your modifier taps:

  • Because this Fish function is internal to the shell, it won't interfere with your Karabiner "Tap to Copy/Undo" rules.
  • The clear command in Fish simply affects the terminal buffer, whereas your Karabiner rules affect the keyboard input level. They will live together in harmony.

Would you like me to help you modify that Fish function so it only clears the screen for specific commands, like git or ls?

To target only ls and git commands in Fish, we can modify the function to inspect the command string before it runs.

The fish_preexec event passes the command string as an argument. We can use a switch statement or a regex match to check if the command starts with your specific targets.

The Fish Configuration

Add this to your ~/.config/fish/config.fish file:

function clear_on_specific_commands --on-event fish_preexec
    # $argv[1] contains the command about to be executed
    switch $argv[1]
        case 'ls*' 'git*'
            clear
    end
end

How this works:

  • ls*: The asterisk is a wildcard. This ensures it clears for ls, ls -la, ls /etc, etc.
  • git*: This covers any git operation, such as git status, git log, or git commit.
  • Selective Clearing: If you run cd, cat, or npm start, your terminal history will remain visible on the screen as usual.

A "Cleaner" Variation

If you want to be more surgical—for example, clearing only for git status but not for git log (so you don't clear the screen only to have git log fill it up again)—you can get more specific with the cases:

function clear_on_specific_commands --on-event fish_preexec
    switch $argv[1]
        case 'ls*' 'git status' 'git diff'
            clear
    end
end

Testing your new setup

After saving the file, run source ~/.config/fish/config.fish in your current terminal.

Since you've been working on those Karabiner rules, this terminal setup creates a very streamlined environment: you can tap Left Control to copy an output, then run ls to instantly get a clean slate for your next task.

Would you like me to show you how to add a "shortcut" to toggle this auto-clearing on and off without editing the file?

turns.prompt_text: Let's auto-ls every time we cd
turns.response_html:
In Fish, the most efficient way to do this is by wrapping the cd command in a function. This ensures that every time the working directory changes—whether you type cd, prevd, or nextd—the ls command is triggered automatically.

The Fish Configuration

Add the following to your ~/.config/fish/config.fish file:

# This function triggers whenever the $PWD (Process Working Directory) variable changes
function auto_ls_on_cd --on-variable PWD
    # Only run if the shell is interactive (prevents issues with scripts)
    if status --is-interactive
        # You can change 'ls' to 'ls -la' or 'exa' if you prefer
        ls
    end
end

Why use --on-variable PWD instead of an alias?

  • Universal: Using a variable watcher means it works even if you use shortcuts like cd - (go back) or if you have other plugins that move you around the file system.
  • Cleaner: You don't have to redefine the cd command itself, which avoids potential conflicts with other shell utilities.

Combining with your "Clear" logic

Since you just set up the auto-clear for ls and git, this creates a powerful workflow:

  1. You type cd projects.
  2. The PWD variable changes.
  3. The auto_ls_on_cd function calls ls.
  4. Your previous function sees the ls command, clears the screen, and then the directory contents are printed at the very top.

Refined "Clear + LS" Setup

If you want to ensure the screen clears specifically when you cd (so you always start at the top of the terminal in a new folder), you can consolidate them like this:

function auto_ls_and_clear_on_cd --on-variable PWD
    if status --is-interactive
        clear
        ls
    end
end

Next Steps

Would you like me to help you customize the ls output (like adding colors or file icons) to make that "fresh" screen look even better?

To achieve this macro sequence in Karabiner-Elements, we can add a new rule to your modular setup. We will use a to array to fire the keystrokes sequentially: ⌘A, ⌘V, and then ⌘S.

Because you mentioned keeping your configuration modular, we will add this right into your existing tap_mods.json file.

Step 1: Update Your Modular File

Replace the contents of ~/.config/karabiner/assets/complex_modifications/tap_mods.json with the updated code block below.

I have added the new Shift + F9 macro rule at the very top of the list so it evaluates first:

{
  "title": "My Custom Tap Modifiers",
  "rules": [
    {
      "description": "F9 Macro and Modifier Taps",
      "manipulators": [
        {
          "description": "Shift + F9 -> Select All, Paste, Save (Cmd+A, Cmd+V, Cmd+S)",
          "type": "basic",
          "from": {
            "key_code": "f9",
            "modifiers": { "mandatory": ["left_shift"], "optional": ["any"] }
          },
          "to": [
            { "key_code": "a", "modifiers": ["left_command"] },
            { "key_code": "v", "modifiers": ["left_command"] },
            { "key_code": "s", "modifiers": ["left_command"] }
          ]
        },
        {
          "description": "Left Command + Shift -> Paste without formatting (Shift+Option+Cmd+V)",
          "type": "basic",
          "from": {
            "key_code": "left_command",
            "modifiers": { "mandatory": ["left_shift"], "optional": ["any"] }
          },
          "to_if_alone": [
            {
              "key_code": "v",
              "modifiers": ["left_command", "left_option", "left_shift"]
            }
          ],
          "to_if_held_down": [{ "key_code": "left_command" }]
        },
        {
          "description": "Left Control -> Copy (Tap)",
          "type": "basic",
          "from": { "key_code": "left_control", "modifiers": { "optional": ["any"] } },
          "to_if_alone": [{ "key_code": "c", "modifiers": ["left_command"] }],
          "to_if_held_down": [{ "key_code": "left_control" }]
        },
        {
          "description": "Left Option -> Cut (Tap)",
          "type": "basic",
          "from": { "key_code": "left_option", "modifiers": { "optional": ["any"] } },
          "to_if_alone": [{ "key_code": "x", "modifiers": ["left_command"] }],
          "to_if_held_down": [{ "left_option" }]
        },
        {
          "description": "Left Command -> Paste (Tap)",
          "type": "basic",
          "from": { "key_code": "left_command", "modifiers": { "optional": ["any"] } },
          "to_if_alone": [{ "key_code": "v", "modifiers": ["left_command"] }],
          "to_if_held_down": [{ "key_code": "left_command" }]
        },
        {
          "description": "Right Command -> Undo (Tap)",
          "type": "basic",
          "from": { "key_code": "right_command", "modifiers": { "optional": ["any"] } },
          "to_if_alone": [{ "key_code": "z", "modifiers": ["left_command"] }],
          "to_if_held_down": [{ "key_code": "right_command" }]
        },
        {
          "description": "Right Option -> Redo (Tap)",
          "type": "basic",
          "from": { "key_code": "right_option", "modifiers": { "optional": ["any"] } },
          "to_if_alone": [
            {
              "key_code": "z",
              "modifiers": ["left_command", "left_shift"]
            }
          ],
          "to_if_held_down": [{ "key_code": "right_option" }]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Step 2: Apply the Changes

  1. Save the file.
  2. Open Karabiner-Elements Settings -> Complex Modifications.
  3. If you already have the old version enabled, click Remove next to it, then click Add rule and re-enable "F9 Macro and Modifier Taps" to force Karabiner to load the fresh JSON logic.

A Quick Note on Mac Function Keys

On a MacBook Air, the function keys default to media controls (like changing brightness or skipping songs).

  • If your Mac is set up so you have to hold the fn key to use F9, your physical combination for this macro will be fn + Shift + F9.
  • If you have "Use F1, F2, etc. keys as standard function keys" turned on in your macOS System Settings, then just Shift + F9 will work natively.

Because Karabiner fires these three commands instantly back-to-back, some heavy IDEs or browsers can occasionally drop a stroke if they are lagging. If you test it out and find that it selects all and pastes but misses the "save" step, we can easily add a few milliseconds of simultaneous_threshold_milliseconds or a tiny internal delay between the keys to stabilize it.

turns.response_html:
Got it. Let’s keep your files perfectly segmented and modular. Since you want to keep your modifier keys separate from your function key macros, we will create a dedicated file just for your F-key actions.

Step 1: Create the New Modular File

Open your terminal and create a new file specifically for these macros:

touch ~/.config/karabiner/assets/complex_modifications/f_keys_macros.json

Step 2: Paste the F-Key Configuration

Paste the following block into ~/.config/karabiner/assets/complex_modifications/f_keys_macros.json. This isolated file handles Shift + F9 without touching your modifier logic.

{
  "title": "F-Key Macro Modifications",
  "rules": [
    {
      "description": "Shift + F9 -> Select All, Paste, Save (Cmd+A, Cmd+V, Cmd+S)",
      "manipulators": [
        {
          "type": "basic",
          "from": {
            "key_code": "f9",
            "modifiers": { "mandatory": ["left_shift"], "optional": ["any"] }
          },
          "to": [
            { "key_code": "a", "modifiers": ["left_command"] },
            { "key_code": "v", "modifiers": ["left_command"] },
            { "key_code": "s", "modifiers": ["left_command"] }
          ]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Step 3: Enable the New Rule in the GUI

  1. Open Karabiner-Elements Settings.
  2. Go to the Complex Modifications tab.
  3. Click Add rule at the bottom.
  4. You will now see a distinct section titled "F-Key Macro Modifications".
  5. Click Enable next to the Shift + F9 rule.

Now your project organization is clean: your modifier taps live in one file, and your functional text/document macros live in another.

If Karabiner swallows the keystrokes too quickly for your editor to process the text insertion before saving, let me know; we can introduce a sequence delay right here in this file to give the clipboard buffer a split-second to breathe.
